entries.meaning: An increase in amount, value, or advantage. ---
examples: The fund posted a small gain last quarter.
Both parties made gains in the suburbs.
Any gain in speed costs you accuracy.

entries.meaning: The way a person or animal walks. ---
examples: I recognized him by his rolling gait.
The therapist is working on her gait after surgery.
A horse has four natural gaits.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like gate.

entries.meaning: An informal American word for a girl or woman. ---
examples: She's the gal who fixed my truck.
A couple of gals from work came along.
He's looking for a gal who likes fishing.
entries.contrast: Casual and a little old-fashioned; in writing use woman.

entries.meaning: Rude boldness; the nerve to do something shocking. ---
examples: He had the gall to ask for a raise that same week.
I can't believe the gall of these people.
She had the gall to show up uninvited.

entries.meaning: The fastest running pace of a horse. ---
examples: The horse broke into a gallop across the field.
She rode at a full gallop down the beach.
The trainer gives him two easy gallops a week.

entries.meaning: A small hard lump that forms in the gallbladder and can cause severe pain. ---
examples: The scan showed a large gallstone.
She had her gallbladder out because of gallstones.
A gallstone can block the duct and bring on an attack.

entries.meaning: A clever opening move meant to gain an advantage, in chess or in a negotiation. ---
examples: His opening gambit was to offer half of what they asked.
The lawsuit was a gambit to delay the sale.
She's tried all the usual gambits to get out of chores.

entries.meaning: A risky action taken in the hope of a good result. ---
examples: Quitting his job was a gamble that paid off.
Opening a restaurant is always a gamble.
They took a few gambles and lost most of them.

entries.meaning: Someone who plays games of chance for money, especially often. ---
examples: Her father was a gambler who lost the house.
The casino watches its biggest gamblers closely.
He's a careful gambler who never bets the rent.

entries.meaning: The activity of betting money on games or events. ---
examples: Online gambling is legal in some states.
Gambling cost him his savings.
The town depends on gambling for tax revenue.

entries.meaning: A sex cell, such as an egg or a sperm, that joins with another to form a new organism. ---
examples: Each gamete carries half the usual number of chromosomes.
In humans the gametes are eggs and sperm.
The lab can freeze a gamete for years.

entries.meaning: The third letter of the Greek alphabet, used in science to label a third kind of something. ---
examples: The symbol on the board is a lowercase gamma.
Gamma rays carry far more energy than X-rays.
He labeled the third curve with a gamma.

entries.meaning: The whole range of something, from one extreme to the other. ---
examples: Her reaction ran the gamut from shock to laughter.
The menu covers the whole gamut of comfort food.
Prices run the gamut at that store.

entries.meaning: The decay of body tissue that happens when blood stops reaching it. ---
examples: Gangrene set in and they had to amputate.
The wound got infected and turned to gangrene.
Diabetes raises the risk of gangrene in the feet.

entries.meaning: A member of an organized group of violent criminals. ---
examples: The movie is about a young gangster in 1930s Chicago.
Two gangsters were arrested at the airport.
He dressed like a gangster for Halloween.

entries.meaning: A bush with thick white flowers that smell very sweet. ---
examples: A single gardenia perfumed the whole room.
Gardenias need acidic soil and a lot of patience.
She wore a gardenia in her hair.

entries.meaning: A deep red gemstone, the birthstone for January. ---
examples: Her ring has a small garnet in the center.
He collects garnets and other semiprecious stones.
The pendant is an antique garnet set in gold.
entries.contrast: The stone is a garnet; the red fruit with the same name in Russian is a pomegranate.

entries.meaning: A group of soldiers stationed in a town or fort, or the place where they stay. ---
examples: A small garrison held the fort all winter.
The army closed three garrisons last year.
News reached the garrison two days later.

entries.meaning: A band worn around the leg to hold up a stocking. ---
examples: The bride wore a blue garter under her dress.
Old photographs show men wearing sock garters.
She keeps her grandmother's lace garter in a box.
entries.contrast: A garter snake is a harmless striped snake, not a piece of clothing.

entries.meaning: A lamp that burns gas, or the light such a lamp gives. ---
examples: The old street is still lit by gaslights.
They read by gaslight before the town had electricity.
A single gaslight flickered at the end of the alley.
entries.contrast: Modern English also uses gaslight as a verb: to make someone doubt their own memory.

entries.meaning: A quick, sharp breath taken in surprise, pain, or shock. ---
examples: A gasp went through the courtroom.
She let out a gasp when she saw the price.
There were gasps from the audience at the ending.

entries.meaning: Someone who controls who or what is allowed through or in. ---

Editors used to be the gatekeepers of publishing.

entries.meaning: An entrance, or something that leads on to something bigger. ---
examples: St. Louis calls itself the gateway to the West.
A stone gateway leads into the garden.
For some kids, vaping is a gateway to smoking.

entries.meaning: Gauntlet has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The knight's gauntlet was dented from the fight.
Welders wear leather gauntlets.
He pulled off one gauntlet to shake hands.
Every nominee has to run the gauntlet of Senate hearings.
Reporters formed a gauntlet the mayor had to walk through.
Getting the permit meant a gauntlet of city offices and forms.

senses.head: A heavy protective glove that covers part of the arm
examples: The knight's gauntlet was dented from the fight.
Welders wear leather gauntlets.
He pulled off one gauntlet to shake hands.

senses.head: A painful ordeal made up of one attack or test after another
examples: Every nominee has to run the gauntlet of Senate hearings.
Reporters formed a gauntlet the mayor had to walk through.
Getting the permit meant a gauntlet of city offices and forms.

entries.русский: латная перчатка; краги; тяжёлое испытание, полоса нападок

entries.meaning: A long, steady look at someone or something. ---
examples: She met his gaze without blinking.
His gaze drifted back to the window.
I felt their gazes on me as I walked in.

entries.meaning: A newspaper, especially one that prints official announcements. ---
examples: The story ran in the local gazette.
He kept old gazettes from the 1940s in the attic.
Almost every county here has a gazette of some kind.
entries.contrast: Mostly survives in newspaper names; the everyday word is newspaper.

entries.meaning: A cold Spanish soup made from raw tomatoes, cucumber, and peppers. ---
examples: We had gazpacho on the patio.
Her gazpacho has too much garlic for me.
Gazpacho is perfect on a hot August day.

entries.meaning: Someone with an intense, expert interest in a subject, especially computers. ---
examples: My roommate is a total computer geek.
The geeks in the IT room fixed it in a minute.
I'm a geek about old maps.
entries.contrast: Once an insult, now usually friendly or even proud.

entries.meaning: An old man, especially one seen as odd or grumpy. ---
examples: Some geezer yelled at us for parking there.
He calls himself an old geezer now.
A couple of geezers play chess in the park every morning.
entries.contrast: In American English a geezer is an old man; in British slang it just means a guy.

entries.meaning: A Japanese woman trained to entertain guests with music, dance, and conversation. ---
examples: A geisha poured the tea and began to play.
The book follows a young geisha in Kyoto.
Real geishas are rare today.

entries.meaning: A clear substance made from animal bones that makes liquid set into a soft solid. ---
examples: Sprinkle the gelatin over cold water first.
Marshmallows are made with gelatin.
Vegetarians look for desserts without gelatin.
entries.contrast: American gelatin, British gelatine.

entries.meaning: A unit inside a cell that carries information passed from parents to children. ---
examples: Scientists identified the gene linked to the disease.
You get half your genes from each parent.
It's in his genes — his whole family is tall.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like jean, as in a pair of jeans.

entries.meaning: The study of family history, or a record of who descended from whom. ---
examples: She got into genealogy after a DNA test.
The library has genealogies of most local families.
Tracing his genealogy took him back to 1740.
entries.contrast: Spelled -alogy, not -ology, though it sounds like the other -ology words.

entries.meaning: A scientist who studies genes and how traits are inherited. ---
examples: A geneticist at the university explained the results.
Geneticists have mapped the whole human genome.
She trained as a geneticist before going into medicine.

entries.meaning: A magical spirit in stories that appears from a lamp or bottle and grants wishes. ---
examples: If a genie gave you three wishes, what would you ask for?
The kids drew genies coming out of lamps.
That genie is out of the bottle now.

entries.meaning: The complete set of genes in a living thing. ---
examples: The human genome was first mapped in 2003.
They sequenced the virus's genome in two days.
The genomes of related species overlap heavily.

entries.meaning: A polite word for a man, or a man who behaves well toward others. ---
examples: A gentleman at the counter is asking for you.
Ladies and gentlemen, please take your seats.
He held the door for her — a real gentleman.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural gentlemen; both forms end in the same -muhn sound.

entries.meaning: A kind, careful way of treating people or things. ---
examples: He handled the puppy with surprising gentleness.
Her gentleness with the patients was obvious.

entries.meaning: A plain-looking rock that is hollow inside and lined with crystals. ---

entries.meaning: Someone who studies the earth's surface and how people live on it. ---

She works as a geographer for the census bureau.

entries.meaning: The way geography and national interests shape relations between countries. ---

The course covers the geopolitics of the Arctic.

entries.meaning: The branch of medicine that deals with the health of older people. ---
examples: She specialized in geriatrics after her residency.
Geriatrics is a growing field as the population ages.

entries.contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb, like physics.

entries.meaning: A voting district drawn with unfair boundaries to help one political party win. ---

Both parties have drawn gerrymanders when they had the votes.

entries.contrast: More often used as a verb (to gerrymander) or as gerrymandering.

entries.meaning: Butter that has been melted and strained, used in Indian cooking. ---
examples: Fry the onions in ghee instead of oil.

entries.meaning: A small cucumber pickled whole. ---

entries.contrast: The gh is a plain hard g: GUR-kin.

entries.meaning: An evil spirit in stories that robs graves and eats the dead. ---

entries.meaning: An imaginary person of enormous size, or any unusually large person or company. ---

entries.meaning: Speech or writing that makes no sense at all. ---

He was talking gibberish by the third hour.

entries.meaning: A small ape with very long arms that swings through the trees of Southeast Asia. ---

Gibbons sing to mark their territory.
The zoo's new gibbon was born in April.
entries.contrast: Hard g here (GIH-buhn), unlike gibberish.

She simmers the giblets to make gravy.
There's a bag of giblets tucked inside the bird.
entries.contrast: Soft g (JIH-bluht), and almost always plural: giblets.

One gigabit is an eighth of a gigabyte.
entries.contrast: A gigabit is eight times smaller than a gigabyte: speeds use bits, file sizes use bytes.

entries.meaning: A unit of frequency equal to one billion cycles per second, used for processor and radio speeds. ---
examples: The laptop runs at three gigahertz.
Wi-Fi uses the 2.4 and 5 gigahertz bands.
One gigahertz used to be impressive.
entries.contrast: The plural is the same word: five gigahertz, never gigahertzes.

entries.meaning: A short, high laugh, often a nervous or silly one. ---

entries.meaning: A sweet spiced cake or cookie flavored with ginger and molasses. ---

entries.meaning: A hard, crisp cookie flavored with ginger. ---
examples: He dunked a gingersnap in his coffee.

entries.meaning: An ancient Asian tree with fan-shaped leaves, often planted along city streets. ---

entries.meaning: The root of an Asian plant, taken as a medicine or tonic. ---
examples: He drinks ginseng tea every morning.

senses.head: A woman's close female friend
examples: She's out to dinner with her girlfriends.
My mom takes a trip with three girlfriends every fall.
I called my oldest girlfriend the minute I heard the news.

entries.meaning: A man in ancient Rome trained to fight others for public entertainment. ---

Gladiators fought with nets, swords, and tridents.

examples: There's not much glamor in a twelve-hour shift.

entries.meaning: A quick look at someone or something. ---

examples: We watched a glassblower shape a vase in about ten minutes.

entries.meaning: An eye disease in which pressure inside the eye slowly damages vision. ---

examples: There was still a gleam of hope that the deal would go through.

entries.meaning: Someone who travels to many different countries. ---

examples: There's a plastic gnome by the front steps.

entries.contrast: The g is silent: NOHM.

entries.meaning: A large African antelope with a heavy head and curved horns. ---
examples: A herd of gnus crossed the river.

entries.contrast: The g is silent: NOO. Americans usually call this animal a wildebeest.

entries.meaning: An ugly, mischievous creature in folklore and fantasy stories. ---
examples: The kids dressed as goblins for Halloween.

entries.meaning: The act of demanding something firmly and repeatedly. ---
examples: At his mother's insistence, he finally saw a doctor.
Her insistence on doing everything herself wore her out.
The contract was signed at the bank's insistence.

entries.meaning: Rude, disrespectful behavior toward someone in authority. ---
examples: He was sent to the principal for insolence.
The sergeant would not tolerate insolence from a recruit.
There was a quiet insolence in the way she shrugged.

entries.meaning: A person who regularly cannot fall asleep. ---
examples: He's been an insomniac since his twenties.
The app was designed by an insomniac for other insomniacs.
Most insomniacs try everything before they see a specialist.

entries.meaning: An official whose job is to check that rules and standards are being followed. ---
examples: The health inspector shut the kitchen down for a week.
Building inspectors come out on Thursday.
The inspector found a crack in the foundation.

entries.meaning: The feeling that makes you want to create something, or a person or thing that gives you that feeling. ---
examples: She sat at the piano waiting for inspiration.
His grandmother was an inspiration to the whole family.
The desert landscape was one of the painter's main inspirations.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The condition of being likely to change suddenly or to fall apart. ---
examples: Political instability has scared away investors.
The doctor is worried about the instability in his knee.
Years of instability followed the collapse of the currency.

entries.meaning: The person who starts trouble or persuades others to do something bad. ---
examples: Police arrested three men they described as the instigators.
He swears he was a bystander, not the instigator.
The instigator of the prank was never identified.

entries.meaning: An organization set up for research, teaching, or a special purpose. ---
examples: She works at a cancer research institute in Houston.
The institute publishes a report every fall.
Several institutes share the same campus.

entries.meaning: A statement telling you what to do, or, as an uncountable noun, the act of teaching. ---
examples: Follow the instructions on the back of the box.
He received no instruction in how to use the machine.
Her only instruction was to lock the door behind us.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A hormone that controls the level of sugar in the blood, also given as medicine. ---
examples: He takes insulin twice a day.
The price of insulin has become a political issue.
Her body stopped producing insulin when she was nine.

entries.meaning: A rude remark meant to hurt or offend someone. ---
examples: Calling his cooking edible was a real insult.
They traded insults across the parking lot.
The low offer felt like an insult after twenty years of work.
entries.contrast: The noun is IN-sult; the verb is in-SULT: That was an insult. / Don't insult me.

entries.meaning: An organized armed rebellion against a government. ---
examples: The insurgency has lasted more than a decade.
Aid workers left when the insurgency spread north.
Both insurgencies began in poor rural provinces.

entries.meaning: A person who fights against the government of their own country. ---
examples: Insurgents took control of the airport overnight.
The captured insurgent was questioned for hours.
Aid convoys were stopped by insurgents on the highway.

entries.meaning: Intake has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The doctor told him to cut his salt intake.
Track your water intake for a week.
Her calorie intake is about eighteen hundred a day.
Leaves had blocked the water intake.
He installed a cold-air intake on the truck.
Snow packed into the intake and stalled the engine.

senses.head: The amount of food, drink, or air taken into the body
examples: The doctor told him to cut his salt intake.
Track your water intake for a week.
Her calorie intake is about eighteen hundred a day.

senses.head: An opening or pipe through which air, water, or fuel enters an engine or system
examples: Leaves had blocked the water intake.
He installed a cold-air intake on the truck.
Snow packed into the intake and stalled the engine.

entries.meaning: A whole number, with nothing after a decimal point. ---
examples: Three and negative seven are integers; 2.5 is not.
The function only accepts an integer.
Fifth graders learn to add and subtract integers.

entries.meaning: A person whose work and interests center on ideas and serious thinking. ---
examples: He was the leading intellectual of his generation.
A group of intellectuals signed the open letter.
She's an intellectual, but she never talks down to anyone.

entries.meaning: The strength or force of something such as light, feeling, or effort. ---
examples: The storm gained intensity overnight.
He plays with an intensity that wears out his teammates.
The intensity of the pain surprised her.

entries.meaning: What a person means to do, especially as it matters in law. ---
examples: He was charged with assault with intent to kill.
The letter makes his intent perfectly clear.
Whatever the intent, the effect was to shut people out.

entries.meaning: An occasion when two people or things act on or communicate with each other. ---
examples: Their only interaction was a nod in the hallway.
The app tracks every interaction with a customer.
Some interactions between these two drugs are dangerous.

entries.meaning: Sexual activity between people, or, in older writing, dealings between groups. ---
examples: The class covers how diseases spread through intercourse.
The treaty opened up trade and intercourse between the colonies.
She asked her doctor whether intercourse was safe after surgery.

entries.meaning: A doctor who specializes in the medical treatment of adults. ---
examples: My internist handles everything except my knees.
The clinic is hiring two more internists.
She saw an internist before she was sent to a cardiologist.

entries.meaning: The imprisonment of people, often without trial, especially during a war. ---
examples: The museum documents the internment of Japanese Americans.
His grandparents spent the war years in internment.
Congress later apologized for the internment.

entries.meaning: The way two or more things affect each other. ---
examples: The book is about the interplay between climate and migration.
There's a nice interplay of light and shadow in that photo.
The interplay among the three lead actors carries the film.

entries.meaning: Something that stops an activity for a while, or the act of breaking in on someone. ---
examples: She worked for six hours without a single interruption.
Sorry for the interruption — one quick question.
Constant interruptions make it impossible to concentrate.

entries.meaning: Intervention has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The family staged an intervention to get him into treatment.
Early intervention makes a big difference for these kids.
The bank survived only because of government intervention.
His sisters staged an intervention over Thanksgiving.
A counselor walked the family through how an intervention works.
After the intervention he agreed to go to rehab.

senses.head: An action taken to change what is happening, especially to help or to stop harm
examples: The family staged an intervention to get him into treatment.
Early intervention makes a big difference for these kids.
The bank survived only because of government intervention.

senses.head: A planned meeting in which family and friends confront someone about a drinking or drug problem
examples: His sisters staged an intervention over Thanksgiving.
A counselor walked the family through how an intervention works.
After the intervention he agreed to go to rehab.

entries.meaning: The person who is being interviewed. ---
examples: Each interviewee gets thirty minutes with the panel.
Half the interviewees said they would move for the job.
The interviewee asked whether the position was remote.
entries.contrast: The interviewer asks the questions; the interviewee answers them.

entries.meaning: The use of threats or fear to make someone do what you want. ---
examples: Voters reported intimidation outside the polling place.
The lawsuit accuses the company of intimidation of witnesses.
He ran the shop through intimidation rather than respect.

entries.meaning: An unwillingness to accept other people's beliefs, or a body's inability to handle a certain food. ---
examples: The speech was a warning against religious intolerance.
She has a lactose intolerance and avoids milk.
Intolerance of any kind was not allowed in that classroom.

entries.meaning: The state of being drunk or affected by a drug or poison. ---
examples: The report listed intoxication as a factor in the crash.
He was treated for alcohol intoxication at the emergency room.
The officer noted clear signs of intoxication.

entries.meaning: A private computer network inside a company that outsiders cannot reach. ---
examples: The forms are on the company intranet.
You can only open that page from the intranet.
Both offices run on the same intranet.
entries.contrast: Intranet (internal, one company) is one letter from Internet (public, worldwide).

entries.meaning: Secret plotting and scheming, especially for power. ---
examples: The court was full of gossip and intrigue.
The novel mixes romance with political intrigue.
There's more intrigue in that office than in a spy movie.
entries.contrast: The noun is usually IN-treeg; the verb to intrigue (to fascinate) is in-TREEG.

entries.meaning: A short opening part of a song, talk, or piece of writing. ---
examples: Everybody knows that guitar intro.
Skip the intro and get to the point.
The podcast's intros are all about a minute long.

entries.meaning: The tendency to be quiet and to prefer being alone rather than in groups. ---
examples: The test measures introversion along with four other traits.
Her introversion was mistaken for coldness.
Introversion is not the same thing as shyness.

entries.meaning: A person who is quiet and gets tired by too much company. ---
examples: As an introvert, he needs a whole day alone after a party.
The office layout is hard on introverts.
She's an introvert who happens to be good on stage.

entries.meaning: Someone who enters a place without permission. ---
examples: The dog barked and the intruder ran.
The alarm alerts you to intruders in the yard.
Police believe the intruder came in through a basement window.

entries.meaning: An unwanted entry into a place or into someone's private life. ---
examples: She called the reporters' questions an intrusion.
The system logs every intrusion attempt.
Small intrusions on his time added up to lost hours.

entries.meaning: An army, country, or organism that enters a place by force. ---
examples: The city held out against the invaders for a year.
Zebra mussels are an invader from the Black Sea.
The invaders burned the fields as they retreated.

entries.meaning: A person who is too ill or weak to look after themselves. ---
examples: After the stroke he lived as an invalid for six years.
The house was designed for an aging invalid.
She refused to be treated like an invalid.
entries.contrast: The noun is IN-vuh-lid (a sick person); the adjective invalid (not valid) is in-VAL-id.

entries.meaning: A person who creates something that did not exist before. ---
examples: The inventor of the zipper never got rich from it.
Two inventors are listed on the patent.
He calls himself an inventor, but mostly he fixes lawn mowers.

entries.meaning: The exact opposite or reverse of something, especially in mathematics. ---
examples: Division is the inverse of multiplication.
Her argument is simply the inverse of his.
Find the inverse of the function and graph it.

entries.meaning: Inversion has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A temperature inversion traps smog over the valley.
The sentence uses an inversion for emphasis.
The plot depends on a series of inversions.
An inversion held the smoke over the valley for a week.
Air quality drops whenever a winter inversion settles in.
The forecast calls for an inversion through Thursday.

senses.head: A reversal of the usual order or position of things
examples: A temperature inversion traps smog over the valley.
The sentence uses an inversion for emphasis.
The plot depends on a series of inversions.

senses.head: A layer of warm air that traps cooler air and smog near the ground
examples: An inversion held the smoke over the valley for a week.
Air quality drops whenever a winter inversion settles in.
The forecast calls for an inversion through Thursday.

entries.meaning: An animal without a backbone, such as an insect, worm, or jellyfish. ---
examples: Most of the animals on earth are invertebrates.
The tide pool is full of tiny invertebrates.
A squid is an invertebrate, even though it's large and smart.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to find out the facts about a crime or an accident. ---
examples: Federal investigators arrived the next morning.
The lead investigator would not comment.
She hired a private investigator to find her brother.

entries.meaning: The state of not being able to be seen or noticed. ---
examples: The cloak gives the wearer invisibility.
She writes about the invisibility of older women on screen.
Invisibility has its advantages in a big office.

entries.meaning: A prayer or formal appeal at the start of a ceremony, or the use of a law or right. ---
examples: A local pastor gave the invocation before the meeting.
His invocation of the Fifth Amendment surprised no one.
The ceremony opens with two short invocations.
entries.русский: призыв, обращение (к высшим силам); ссылка на закон

entries.meaning: The fact of taking part in something or being connected with it. ---
examples: He denied any involvement in the robbery.
Parent involvement is what makes the program work.
Her involvement with the charity goes back twenty years.

entries.meaning: The process by which atoms gain or lose electrons and become charged. ---
examples: Ionization happens when the gas is heated enough.
The detector measures the ionization caused by the particle.
We covered ionization in the second week of chemistry.

entries.meaning: The layer of the upper atmosphere that reflects radio waves. ---
examples: Shortwave signals bounce off the ionosphere.
Solar storms disturb the ionosphere and disrupt radio traffic.
The satellite studies the lower ionosphere.

entries.meaning: A very small amount, usually used in negative sentences. ---
examples: He hasn't changed one iota since high school.
There isn't an iota of evidence for that claim.
It didn't help their case one iota.

entries.meaning: A signed note saying that you owe someone money. ---
examples: He left an IOU for twenty dollars on the counter.
The drawer was full of old IOUs from his brother.
I'll pay you Friday — here, take an IOU.
entries.contrast: The spelling comes from the sound of I owe you.

entries.meaning: The use of words to mean the opposite of what they say, or a situation that turns out the opposite of what was expected. ---
examples: There's a certain irony in a fire station burning down.
He said it with heavy irony, but she took him seriously.
The irony was lost on everyone in the room.
entries.contrast: Two syllables in the stem: EYE-ruh-nee. Do not say it like iron plus -y.

entries.meaning: Something that does not follow the normal rule or pattern, often something improper. ---
examples: Auditors found several irregularities in the accounts.
The doctor noticed an irregularity in his heartbeat.
Every irregularity in the pavement showed after the rain.

entries.meaning: The quality of having nothing to do with the matter being discussed. ---
examples: The judge pointed out the irrelevance of the question.
The whole department slid into irrelevance after the merger.
He argued the irrelevance of the older studies.

entries.meaning: A lack of respect for things that other people take seriously. ---
examples: The show is famous for its cheerful irreverence.
His irreverence got him in trouble with the older faculty.
There's a healthy irreverence in the way she talks about awards.

entries.meaning: The tendency to get annoyed easily. ---
examples: Irritability is a common side effect of the medication.
Lack of sleep explains most of his irritability.
The doctor asked about mood changes and irritability.

entries.meaning: Something that makes the body sore or that keeps annoying you. ---
examples: Chlorine is a mild irritant to the eyes.
The noise from the construction is a daily irritant.
Avoid soaps with known irritants in them.

entries.meaning: A person who lives on an island. ---
examples: The islanders voted against building the bridge.
As an islander, he had never seen a train.
Most islanders fish or work in tourism.
entries.contrast: The s is silent, as in island: EYE-luhn-dur.

entries.meaning: An island, especially a small one or one named in a title. ---
examples: They honeymooned on a tiny isle off the coast of Maine.
The song calls Ireland the Emerald Isle.
Ferries run between the two isles twice a day.
entries.contrast: The s is silent, so isle sounds exactly like aisle and I'll.

entries.meaning: The state of being kept apart from other people or things. ---
examples: He spent ten days in isolation after the diagnosis.
Rural isolation is hard on older people.
Don't read that sentence in isolation from the rest.

entries.meaning: The policy of staying out of other countries' affairs. ---
examples: American isolationism ended with Pearl Harbor.
The speech was a warning against a return to isolationism.
Critics called the trade policy pure isolationism.

entries.meaning: A narrow strip of land joining two larger areas of land. ---
examples: Panama sits on an isthmus between two oceans.
A road runs the length of the isthmus.
Both isthmuses were cut by canals in the last century.
entries.contrast: The th is silent: ISS-muhs, not ISTH-mus.

entries.meaning: One version of something in a series of repeated attempts or improvements.
examples: This is the third iteration of the design.
Each iteration of the app got a little faster.
We went through six iterations before the client was happy.
